planting.note: Set dormant rhizomes or potted divisions into deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in dappled or full shade; the emerging lobed leaves and pink flowers appear very early and can be nipped by late frost.

directions: Himalayan mayapple is the single-leaved Asian counterpart to the American Podophyllum, unfurling a pair of glossy, deeply lobed leaves on a short stem with a single nodding pink flower held just above them in early spring. The flower gives way to a showy bright red-orange fruit by midsummer, making this one of the more ornamental members of the mayapple clan. It is slow to establish and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent woodland site with consistent moisture and rich organic matter before planting. Pair it with trilliums, Jeffersonia, or epimediums for an early-season shade display that fades gracefully by midsummer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions or container stock in early spring into deep, moist, humus-rich woodland soil in full to partial shade, away from late-frost pockets.

directions: Native across a broad swath of eastern and southern China as well as Taiwan, Dysosma pleiantha produces a single angular, star-shaped leaf per stem with faint maroon mottling along the veins. Small maroon-red flowers cluster beneath the leaf in spring, largely hidden from above and best enjoyed by tilting the foliage upward, followed by dangling red fruit later in the season. Like other mayapple relatives it needs steady moisture and rich, well-drained humus and dislikes being moved once settled in. Use it as a textural companion to ferns, Disporopsis, or Asarum in a shaded woodland bed.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in early spring into cool, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in deep shade; protect emerging foliage from late frost.

directions: Collected from the mountain forests of Yunnan, Sichuan, Guizhou, and Shaanxi, Dysosma delavayi is a smaller-growing mayapple with a single deeply cut, umbrella-like leaf and dark nodding flowers set low beneath the foliage in spring. It is a choice collector's plant for cool, humid woodland gardens and shares the genus's preference for undisturbed, consistently moist, acidic to neutral soil high in organic matter. Site it where it can be left alone for years, as the shallow rhizomes resent transplanting. Its modest scale makes it a good match for Jeffersonia, Beesia, or small ferns rather than the larger-leaved Podophyllum peltatum.

planting.note: Wedge container-grown rosettes sideways into vertical crevices or steep slopes of tufa, limestone, or well-drained rubble in shade, keeping the crown dry while the roots stay cool and moist.

directions: Endemic to rocky crevices in Serbia, North Macedonia, and northern Greece, Ramonda nathaliae forms a flat rosette of crinkled, dark green leaves topped in late spring by clusters of lilac-blue, flat-faced flowers with contrasting yellow anthers. Like its Pyrenean relative it is a poikilohydric 'resurrection plant' that can withstand near-total desiccation of its leaves and recover fully once rewetted, an adaptation to its exposed limestone cliff habitat. Plant it on a shaded, north-facing rock face or crevice garden wall where winter wet cannot collect around the crown, since standing moisture is more damaging than cold. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliability in cultivation.

planting.note: Tuck rosettes sideways into a shaded, steep limestone crevice or vertical wall with sharp drainage; avoid overhead watering onto the hairy leaves.

directions: First found on the shaded, north-facing limestone cliffs near Nis, Serbia, Ramonda serbica is a close relative of R. nathaliae, distinguished by hairier, more deeply veined leaves and violet flowers with a short, less showy corolla tube. It grows wild in cool, damp, shaded rock crevices where it experiences near-total drying between rains and regenerates once moisture returns, the same resurrection-plant trait shared across the genus. In the garden it wants the same steep, shaded crevice conditions, with roots in a cool, humus-rich crack and the crown protected from winter wet. Grow it alongside Haberlea or saxifrages in a shaded alpine wall for a Balkan crevice-garden theme.

planting.note: Grow year-round in a shallow pot of fast-draining, humus-rich mix in bright shade; treat as a houseplant or terrarium subject outside mild, frost-free climates.

directions: Native to wet, mossy limestone rock faces in Yunnan, China, Petrocosmea forrestii forms a flat rosette of rounded, quilted, dark green leaves closely related in form and care to African violets. Small white to pale lavender flowers with a yellow throat rise just above the foliage on thin stalks for an extended bloom season. Outdoors it suits a shaded, humid rock garden pocket in frost-free climates; elsewhere it is better grown as a terrarium or windowsill specimen in a shallow pan with excellent drainage. Keep water off the leaves and out of the crown to prevent rot, mimicking the brief misting it receives in its native seep-fed cliff habitat.
